first_impression.reaction: My assistant shortlisted it, so I gave it the first screen. 'The ring may be the most valuable thing either of you wears every day, and it is easy to assume it is already covered.' Calm, not gushing, fine. But it's a household insurance explainer: contents policies, Moneysmart, AFCA. Our jewellery is handled by the family office and a specialist broker. I read the takeaways and the travel section and left the rest to my assistant.

journey.quote: This is general information, not financial advice. Read the policy wording, the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS), before you buy.
journey.reaction: Responsible, and I respect that it doesn't pretend to be something it isn't. It also tells me in the first screen this is written for someone buying their own policy, not for us.

journey.quote: A contents policy can cover your ring, but per-item limits mean you may need to add it and check its value against the limit.
journey.reaction: Correct, but basic. Nobody in my family keeps serious jewellery on a home contents policy.

journey.section: Three ways to insure an engagement ring in Australia
journey.quote: If you are still choosing the ring, [deciding how much to spend on a ring you are comfortable insuring](/expert-advice/how-much-should-you-spend-on-an-engagement-ring) is a sensible place to start.
journey.reaction: Spending guidance high up the page. Not offensive, but it signals the reader they have in mind, and it isn't me.

journey.section: Carry-on, travel dates and hotel safes
journey.quote: In practice, the ring is on a hand, in the carry-on or in the room safe.
journey.reaction: Sensible and plainly put. But at our scale the question is the whole family's jewellery, the bridal party's pieces, who carries them, and how the venue's security and ours hand them over. Nothing on that.

journey.section: Carry-on, travel dates and hotel safes
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact, so the logistics around the rings sit inside one plan.
journey.reaction: This is the only line that speaks to what I actually need, a planner who owns logistics. It's understated, which I like. But it doesn't say they've ever handled security, private transfers or a wedding of 300.

journey.section: Water, beach and boat days: swap to a plain band
journey.quote: A simple band for those days, with the engagement ring in the safe, takes that risk off the table.
journey.reaction: Practical. My assistant would pass this on. No complaint.

journey.quote: a Wedded Advisor will plan the venue and the travel with you from first idea to the last dance, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD.
journey.reaction: 'Quoting in AUD' is a small thing, but it reads like a standard client. I'm in Dubai. I want to know what's possible, not what currency the quote comes in.

unanswered_questions: Has Wedded Wonderland handled weddings of 200 to 400 guests with VIP logistics?
Can a Wedded Advisor coordinate the family's own security team with the venue's, including custody of jewellery on the day?
Is there a private or referral channel to speak to someone, rather than a general enquiry form?
How is client privacy and discretion handled (NDAs, no social posting by vendors)?
Does the team work with families based outside Australia, for example in Dubai and London?
would_share_with: My assistant, for the travel and hotel safe points only

cta_reaction.quote: See [how a Wedded Advisor plans the wedding travel](/wonderland-concierge).
cta_reaction.why: Only because it's the one place that points to planning rather than insurance. I'd click it to see whether they look like they handle scale and discretion. I wouldn't enquire from this post; that would come through a private channel or a referral.

top_3_changes: Add one short line in the destination wedding travel section on high-value jewellery for the wider family and bridal party (who carries it, secure handover at the venue), as a question to put to the planner and venue, without inventing services.
Move the 'how much to spend' link out of the opening comparison section to later in the post so the first screens read as expert guidance rather than budget guidance.
In the closing paragraph, consider whether 'quoting in AUD' needs to be there; for overseas families it reads as standard-client language (low priority, not must-fix).
